groups.text: One customer asks for a EURUSD price.
Three providers can quote it.
You want the lowest.
One after another, their times add up: six hundred twenty milliseconds.
Start all three together with async, and you wait only for the slowest: three hundred.
Give the request a deadline: two hundred fifty milliseconds.
Where does the timeout go?
Around the whole fan-out, or around each call?
Around the whole fan-out, the deadline cancels everything.
Northbank and Fjord had answered, and both answers are thrown away.
Around each call, with withTimeoutOrNull, only Eastgate is cut off.
It becomes null.
The answers that arrived still count, and Fjord wins.
Now a rougher run, with no tight deadline.
Northbank fails at fifty milliseconds.
Inside coroutineScope, the three calls are one unit of work.
One failure cancels the others, and the request fails.
A quote needs any one answer.
supervisorScope lets each call fail alone.
At one hundred milliseconds, Fjord's own HTTP client gives up.
It throws TimeoutCancellationException, which is a CancellationException too.
Rethrow every cancel, the usual rule, and Fjord's timeout ends your whole request.
So ask first: was my own coroutine cancelled?
ensureActive throws only if it was, say because the client hung up.
Here it wasn't.
Fjord just has no answer, and Eastgate answers at three hundred.
Last case. All three miss the deadline.
Waiting breaks the deadline, and failing helps nobody.
So serve the last good quote, marked stale, and let the client decide.
Only live answers refresh the cache.
Here it is in Kotlin, with the Java version in Reactor below it.
The rule. Start every call together, give each the deadline, let each fail alone, and rethrow only your own cancel.
Check yourself. You rethrow every CancellationException.
Fjord's client times out at one hundred milliseconds.
What happens to Eastgate's answer at three hundred?
It never counts.
The request fails at one hundred milliseconds with TimeoutCancellationException.
